definition: The federal civilian occupational series for contract specialists and contracting officers.

expansion: Acquisition, Logistics and Technology Contracting NCO
definition: The Army enlisted MOS for contracting NCOs. 51Cs earn the same certification as 1102s and often serve as contingency contracting officers.
An SBA program for small businesses owned by socially and economically disadvantaged people. Contracts can be competed among 8(a) firms or, within limits, awarded sole source through SBA.
The nine-week MOS course at The Army Acquisition School in Huntsville that Soldiers attend when they reclassify into 51C.
The Army command that holds most Army contracting units, including the contracting support brigades where many 51Cs serve.

When an authorized Government representative takes ownership of supplies or approves services as meeting the contract. It is final except for latent defects, fraud, gross mistakes amounting to fraud, or a warranty.
A contracting officer who administers contracts after award, often in a contract administration office such as DCMA.
An agreement that lets U.S. forces and allied militaries exchange logistics support, supplies and services, often used overseas.
The Army's system for writing contracts, orders and modifications. It replaced older systems such as PD2 and SPS-A.
The law that forbids obligating or spending more than is available, or before it is available. Violations must be reported and can bring discipline.

Two or more responsible offerors, competing independently, submit priced offers that meet the requirement, and award is on best value with price a substantial factor. It usually proves a price is reasonable on its own.
A unilateral modification that does not change the parties' rights, such as a new paying office or corrected accounting data.
Ways to settle disagreements without litigation, such as mediation. Encouraged at the contracting officer's level.
The Army's supplement to the FAR and DFARS. Its parts are numbered 5101 to 5153 to match FAR Parts 1 to 53.

expansion: Army training application system in ATRRS
definition: The Army website where acquisition workforce members apply for WarU courses and the certification exam. Requests go to the supervisor and your organization's training approver for approval.
A written plan for how a requirement will be bought: need, strategy, competition, contract type, risks and milestones.
The level of performance below perfect that is still acceptable, used in performance standards for services.

expansion: Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals
definition: The board that hears DoW contractors' appeals of contracting officer final decisions. Appeals are due within 90 days.

expansion: Army Training Requirements and Resources System
definition: The Army's database of record for training, including WarU course and exam registrations.
A fee a contractor earns based on a subjective Government evaluation of its performance, used in cost-plus-award-fee contracts.

expansion: Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement
definition: What you will do if negotiations fail. Knowing it tells you when to walk away.
The expected outcome that provides the greatest overall benefit for the requirement, which may or may not be the lowest price.
An offer submitted in response to an invitation for bids (sealed bidding).
A written understanding with a contractor that sets terms and a method for pricing future orders. It is not a contract; each order is.
The rule that an appropriation may pay only for a genuine need of the period the money is available.
A simplified way to fill repeat needs by setting terms in advance with one or more suppliers. Each call under it is a contract.
A purchase description that names a brand but accepts equal products meeting stated salient characteristics.
Combining requirements into one solicitation in a way likely to be unsuitable for small businesses. It needs market research and a written determination.
A five-character code that identifies a contractor location. It comes with SAM registration.
The Army DACM Office portal for acquisition career records, help requests and related tools.

expansion: Career Acquisition Personnel and Position Management Information System
definition: The Army system that tracks acquisition workforce positions and people.
A change so large it falls outside the general scope of the contract. It is new work that needs its own competition or justification.
Rules for how certain large contractors measure, assign and allocate costs on covered contracts.
DCMA's database for DoW negotiators: contractor business system status, rates and records of negotiations other DoW contracting officers completed.
A contracting officer who buys for deployed forces. Most 51Cs train to serve as CCOs.
The law that governs contract claims: certification over $100,000, contracting officer final decisions, appeals and interest.
The most the Government will pay under a contract, such as on a time-and-materials or incentive contract.
Cost or pricing data the contractor certifies are accurate, complete and current. Required above the TINA threshold unless an exception applies.
A unilateral written order from the contracting officer, under the Changes clause, directing a change within the general scope. The contractor must keep working.
The 1984 law that requires full and open competition unless an exception applies, and creates the automatic stay for timely GAO protests.
Training and development that keeps a certified professional current: 80 hours every 2 years for DoW contracting.
A written demand by a contracting party seeking, as a matter of right, money, an adjustment or interpretation of contract terms, or other relief.
A limited exchange with an offeror, when award without negotiations is planned, to clear up minor issues. It does not let the offeror revise its proposal.
An approved departure from the FAR for a category of actions. DoW used class deviations to adopt the FAR Overhaul from 1 February 2026.
A numbered line in the contract schedule for a separately priced item or service.
The unit used to count continuous learning; usually one point per hour of learning.
Another abbreviation for KO, the official with a warrant to bind the Government.
The federal court that hears bid protests and contract dispute appeals (within 12 months of a final decision).
A product of a type customarily used by the general public or non-Government entities and sold, leased or offered to them, with some allowed modifications.
A service of a type offered and sold competitively in substantial quantities in the commercial marketplace, or one that supports a commercial product.
The evaluated proposals best suited for further negotiation, set when the Government will negotiate with offerors. It may be limited to the most highly rated for an efficient competition.
The contracting officer's written consent before a prime places certain subcontracts. It does not make the Government a party or relieve the prime.
For Prompt Payment purposes, acceptance treated as happening a set number of days after delivery when the Government does not act.
A change the Government causes by words or actions, without a formal change order, that makes the contractor do more or different work.
A military operation designated as one by the Secretary of War or arising under certain laws. With a determination, it raises purchase thresholds.
A temporary law that funds the Government when full appropriations are not passed. It often limits new starts and how much can be obligated.
A mutually binding legal relationship obligating the seller to furnish supplies or services and the buyer to pay for them.
The record of a contract action that must tell its complete story so others can follow every decision.
Financial assistance to carry out a public purpose with substantial Government involvement. Not a contract.
A person the contracting officer designates in writing to monitor technical performance. A COR cannot change the contract.
An oral board that reviews a candidate for a contracting officer warrant in many Army organizations.
Reviewing the separate cost elements and profit in a proposal.
Checking whether proposed costs are realistic for the work, used mainly on cost-reimbursement contracts.
A commercial product sold in substantial quantities and offered without modification. The most streamlined kind of commercial buy.
A cost-reimbursement contract with a fee earned through subjective evaluation of performance.
The system where contracting officers rate contractor performance. Future source selections use the ratings.
A cost-reimbursement contract that pays allowable costs plus a fee set at award.
A cost-reimbursement contract whose fee moves with how actual costs compare with target costs.
A review, done by DCMA in DoW, of how a contractor buys from its subcontractors. An approved system reduces consent requirements.
An Army Contracting Command brigade that provides operational contracting support to an Army service component command, often overseas.
Rules that bar contractors and their employees from trafficking-related activities. They apply to every contract.
A notice giving a contractor at least 10 days to fix a performance failure before a possible termination for default.
The official who runs a military department's acquisition workforce program. The Army DACM Office is part of USAASC.

expansion: Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army (Procurement)
definition: The Army's senior procurement policy official, whose office issues Army contracting policy such as the warranting program.
The former name of WarU, the Warfighting Acquisition University. Older records and certificates may still say DAU.
The law that created the DoW acquisition workforce program, including certification.
The agency that audits contractor proposals, costs and business systems for DoW.
The DoW agency that administers many contracts after award, often at contractor plants.
An explanation to an offeror of why its proposal was excluded or did not win. Postaward requests are due within 3 days of the award notice.
Removing unneeded funds from a contract so they can be used elsewhere while still available.
A written approval in which the findings (facts) support the determination (decision). Some actions require one.
The Department of War's supplement to the FAR. Its parts are numbered 201 to 253.
The DoW agency that pays contractors and keeps the Department's accounts.
A cost tied to a specific contract, such as the labor and materials used on it.
The older name for negotiations with offerors in the competitive range; the RFO FAR calls them competitive negotiations.
The instruction that governs the defense acquisition workforce program: certification, grace periods and continuous learning.
The Department of Defense's secondary name in use since 2025. Rules and offices may say DoD or DoW.

expansion: Defense Pricing, Contracting, and Acquisition Policy
definition: The Pentagon office that sets DoW contracting policy, including the contracting certification requirements.
The Army Contracting Command element that leads expeditionary contracting units.
A PIEE module that stores signed contracts and modifications for viewing.
A fixed-price contract term that adjusts the price for specific market changes, such as fuel or steel prices (see FP-EPA).
A fair change in price, schedule or both to account for a change or other event under the contract.
The system where large contractors report progress on small business subcontracting plans.
A suspension, debarment or other listing in SAM that generally bars a contractor from new awards.
A delay beyond the contractor's control and without its fault, such as acts of God or unusually severe weather. It is not a default.
Appropriations past their period of availability. They can only adjust or pay existing obligations for 5 years, then they cancel.
A numbered release that publishes changes to the FAR.
The civilian agencies' contracting certification. FAC-C (Professional) is treated as equal to the DoW Contracting Professional certification.
A price that is fair to both sides: not too high for the Government and not unrealistically low for the contractor.
The requirement to give each awardee of a multiple-award contract a fair chance to compete for orders, with limited exceptions.
The main rulebook for federal acquisitions with appropriated funds, in 53 parts.
A contract whose price does not change with the contractor's actual costs. The contractor carries the cost risk.
Delivery terms that decide where title and risk of loss pass: at origin (the seller's dock) or at destination.
The law that lets the public request Government records, with exemptions for things like proprietary information.
A trained, appointed person who makes small purchases in the field within written limits, usually paired with a paying agent.
The former contract reporting system. Award reporting moved into SAM.gov in 2026.
A fixed-price contract that adjusts for specific market changes, such as fuel or material prices.
A required source for supplies it makes when market research shows its product is comparable in price, quality and delivery.
A fixed-price contract with a target cost, target profit, ceiling price and share ratio that rewards cost control.
An agreement on a contractor's labor and indirect rates for pricing future contracts over a period.
GSA's long-term contracts for commercial products and services that agencies order from.
All responsible sources may compete. The default rule for Government buys.
The Government's budget year, 1 October to 30 September.
An indirect cost for running the business as a whole, applied to contracts through a rate.
The congressional agency that decides bid protests (within 100 days).
The Army's financial system, where purchase requests and funds are recorded.
Property the Government provides to a contractor for use on a contract.
The Government's charge card, used mainly for micro-purchases by trained cardholders.
Where notices and solicitations are posted: SAM.gov.
The 36 months a new contracting professional has to earn the required certification.
Financial assistance to carry out a public purpose, with no substantial Government involvement. Not a contract.
The agency that runs governmentwide contracts such as the Federal Supply Schedules and GSA Advantage.
GSA's supplement to the FAR. Since the FAR Overhaul, the Federal Supply Schedule ordering procedures live in GSAR subpart 538.71.
The senior official responsible for a contracting activity. Appoints contracting officers and ratifies unauthorized commitments.
An SBA program for small businesses located in and employing people from designated areas.
A contract with a minimum and maximum quantity, filled by orders as needs arise.
Your written plan of training and development, approved by your supervisor.
The solicitation used in sealed bidding. Award goes to the lowest responsive, responsible bidder.
The office that investigates fraud, waste and abuse. You can report wrongdoing to its hotline.
The Government's own estimate of what the work should cost, prepared without contractor input and never shared with offerors.
A cost shared across many contracts, such as overhead or G&A, applied through rates.
A function so tied to the public interest that only Government employees may do it, such as awarding contracts.
The written justification needed to use other than full and open competition, approved at a level set by dollar value.
A PIEE module for DoW appointments such as CORs and purchase card officials.
Two or more businesses that combine to compete for and perform a contract.
Your unit's senior 51C trainer and the person to ask about your certification: the local goal, AITAS, what already counts, who approves what. Also just "the Master Gunner".
The warranted official who can enter into, administer and terminate contracts within the limits of the warrant. Also abbreviated CO.
A 51C or 1102 who prepares and runs contract actions for the contracting officer's decision.
A defect that existed at acceptance but could not be found by a reasonable inspection. Acceptance does not bar remedies for it.
A preliminary contract that lets work start at once, to be definitized later. Tightly limited.
Like time-and-materials, but without materials: payment by fixed hourly rates.
The clause on incrementally funded cost-type contracts that makes the contractor warn the Government before funds run out.
The funding data that shows which appropriation and account pay for a contract line.
A source selection approach: award to the lowest-priced offer that meets every requirement, with no tradeoffs. DoW limits its use.
IDIQ contracts awarded to several companies for the same requirement, who then compete for orders.
Collecting and analyzing information about capabilities in the market that could meet the need.
A memo that documents what happened, when, who decided and why.
The Army Contracting Command element that supports Army installations in the United States.
A purchase at or below the micro-purchase threshold, often made with the purchase card without competitive quotes.
Appropriations for building military facilities, generally available for 5 years.
A DoW form used to send funds and a requirement to another military department or agency.
The record of inspection and acceptance of supplies, now done as a receiving report in PIEE.
Any written change to a contract's terms, made only by a contracting officer, usually on an SF 30.
The dollar ceiling for micro-purchases: $15,000 (higher for contingency and emergency buys).
Industry codes. The code the contracting officer picks sets the SBA size standard for the buy.
An agreement to protect another party's confidential information, common among teaming partners.
The yearly defense law that often changes acquisition rules and thresholds.
An agreement recognizing a successor in interest to a Government contract, such as after a business is sold.
A legal commitment of Government funds, such as signing a contract or order.
When a contractor's other work could impair its objectivity or give it an unfair advantage.
Planning and managing contracted support for military operations.
A response to a solicitation that, if accepted, binds the offeror. Quotes under an RFQ are not offers.
Appropriations for day-to-day operations, generally available for 1 year.
Pearson VUE's online, remotely proctored testing. Most government computers block it, so test centers are recommended.
A unilateral right in a contract for the Government to buy more or extend the term, within set time limits and conditions.
A flexible agreement outside the FAR, used under specific laws such as prototype projects.
Indirect costs such as facilities and supervision, spread across work through a rate.
A trained, appointed person who pays cash for field purchases under strict controls.
The time from receiving a complete requirement package to award.
Buying services by results, with measurable standards and a surveillance plan.
A financial interest or relationship of a contractor employee that could affect their work on Government acquisitions.
The contracting officer who awards the contract.
An SBA representative who reviews acquisitions for small business opportunities.
An older DoW contract writing system, replaced in the Army by ACWS.
The testing company that delivers the CON 3990V certification exam at test centers or online.
The DFARS companion with how-to guidance. It is not regulation.
When all supplies are delivered and services performed and accepted, and no options remain. It starts the closeout clock.
The law that protects bid, proposal and source selection information and governs employment contacts with offerors.
DoW's single sign-on for procurement tools such as WAWF, EDA and JAM.

The Governmentwide-unique number on every solicitation, contract, agreement and order: 13 to 17 characters, starting with the issuing office's activity address code, then the fiscal year, an instrument letter in position 9 (Table 4-1) and a serial number.
The person responsible for a program's cost, schedule and performance.
The record of a negotiation: objectives, positions, the agreement and the reasons.
An offer by the Government to buy, usually under simplified procedures. A contract forms when the vendor accepts.
The law requiring payment generally within 30 days of a proper invoice or acceptance, with automatic interest if late.
The customer's request to buy something, with funds certified.
A written objection by an interested party to a solicitation or award, filed with the agency, GAO or the Court of Federal Claims.
A requirement document that states results and how they will be measured, leaving the method to the contractor.
The Government person who inspects a contractor's work for conformance. A QAR has no authority to change the contract.
The Government's plan for checking a contractor's performance on services.
Approval, by an official with authority, of an unauthorized commitment after the fact, when six conditions are met.
Appropriations for developing new capabilities, generally available for 2 years.
A contractor's request for a price or schedule adjustment that is not yet a formal claim.
A contract to fill all of the Government's actual needs for an item or service during a period from one contractor.
Able to perform: adequate resources, a good record, integrity, and the needed skills and facilities. Required before any award.
In sealed bidding, a bid that complies in all material respects with the invitation for bids.
A notice asking industry for information during market research. It does not solicit offers.
The 2025 to 2026 rewrite and renumbering of the FAR. DoW applies it through class deviations effective 1 February 2026 while formal rules are finalized.
The solicitation used in negotiated acquisitions. Proposals are offers.
The solicitation used in simplified acquisitions. Quotes are not offers.
The finance person who certifies that funds are available.
Above the micro-purchase threshold, set aside for small business when two or more responsible small businesses are expected to offer at fair market prices.
The site for contractor registration, exclusions, contract opportunities and award data.
Streamlined methods for buys at or below the SAT (and commercial buys up to $9 million).
$350,000 (higher for contingency and emergency buys). Below it, simplified procedures apply.
The agency that sets size standards and runs the 8(a), HUBZone and other small business programs.
The senior official responsible for contracting in an organization, such as a contracting support brigade.
A small business owned and controlled by service-disabled veterans, with its own set-aside and sole-source rules.
Reserving a competition for small businesses (or a program like HUBZone). It is still full and open competition among those firms.
A continuing service, such as maintenance, that is a need of the period when it is performed.
The contracting officer's warrant, which states the limits of the authority.

expansion: Solicitation/Contract/Order for Commercial Products and Commercial Services
definition: The standard form for commercial solicitations and contracts.
The standard form for amendments and modifications.
A combined order, invoice and voucher for small over-the-counter buys delivered on the spot, common in the field.
A notice asking a contractor to explain why it should not be terminated for default, used when there is no time for a cure notice.
A breakdown of a contract line item for identification or funding.
An agreement with a host nation that sets the legal status of U.S. forces there. It can affect contracting overseas.
Soliciting and negotiating with only one source. Needs a statutory exception and, above the SAT, a justification.
A short statement of the Government's goals; offerors propose their own PWS.
Information prepared for evaluating offers, such as ratings and rankings, protected from disclosure before award.
A requirement document that describes the work and often how to do it.
The senior official responsible for an agency's acquisition system; the top tier for approving large justifications.
The system that tracks contractor personnel supporting U.S. forces overseas.
A DoW system with supplier risk data, including cybersecurity assessment scores.
The official who makes the source selection decision; often the contracting officer.
The written record of the source selection authority's decision and the rationale for any tradeoffs.
The team that evaluates proposals against the stated factors.
A contracting officer's order to stop all or part of the work for up to 90 days.
A large business's plan for using small business subcontractors, required above set thresholds.
A bilateral modification signed by both the contractor and the contracting officer.
Ending all or part of a contract because it is in the Government's interest, paying for work done and a profit on it.
Ending a contract because the contractor failed to perform. Usually preceded by a cure or show cause notice.
The school in Huntsville that runs the 51C Army Acquisition Transition Course.
Requirements and approvals for contractors working in an overseas operational area.
A contracting officer who settles terminated contracts.

expansion: Truthful Cost or Pricing Data (formerly the Truth in Negotiations Act)
definition: The statute requiring certified cost or pricing data above a threshold unless an exception applies. DoW's threshold is $10 million for awards after 30 June 2026.
Payment by hourly rates plus materials at cost. Least preferred; needs a determination and a ceiling price.
A source selection approach that can award to other than the lowest price when a better offer is worth it.
A contract action that lets work start before the terms and price are agreed. DoW limits and closely watches UCAs.
The standard organization of larger solicitations and contracts, including instructions and evaluation factors.
The 12-character identifier SAM assigns to every registered entity. It replaced the DUNS number.
Money obligated on a contract but not yet paid out. Old ULOs are a sign of contracts needing closeout.
An agreement that is not binding only because the Government person who made it lacked authority.
Line item prices significantly overstated or understated even though the total looks acceptable.
The organization that houses the Army DACM Office and supports the Army acquisition workforce.
The Army's contracting tools, including the Paperless Contract File and the warrant application process.
The written appointment (SF 1402) that gives a contracting officer authority and states its limits.
A promise about the quality or performance of what is delivered, giving the Government remedies after acceptance.
The DoW school, formerly DAU, that teaches the certification courses and owns the certification exam.
The PIEE module for electronic invoices and receiving reports.
A small business at least 51% owned and controlled by women, with its own set-aside rules (also EDWOSB for economically disadvantaged).
